utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Judge Morrison is indisposed today, so therefore we are sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis. Probably Dr. Karadzic needs to introduce his -- or Mr. Robinson, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, Mr. President. We have with us Dr. Dusan Dunjic who's an expert being allowed by the Court to assist us during the testimony of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. If the witness could take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. Please make yourself comfortable. Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Good morning, professor.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can you please state your full name.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Richard Vernon Stafford Wright, with a W.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay, just two things before we start. Could you tell the Court what the papers are that you've got in front of you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: The papers I have in front of me are reports that I wrote for ICTY on the exhumations that I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can I please have 65 ter number 3452 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could we ask the witness to speak closer to the mike. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And, professor, you provided a current copy of your CV to the OTP in November. Is this the CV on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes, but I'd have to see the date at the end to be sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Go to the last page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's the one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you've talked about your background at length in the Krstic trial, and that's the transcript that we are going to be tendering later, but I do want to ask you a couple of questions about your background.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If we can go back to the first page of the CV.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Professor, we see that you're an Emeritus Professor of Anthropology from the University of Sydney, but you're actually an archaeologist; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes, I'm an archaeologist.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can you explain how that works, the difference between your title and your profession?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Well, there really isn't any difference, because in those days the University of Sydney had a Department of Anthropology that included physical anthropology and archaeology and cultural anthropology. So there was -- anthropology was an umbrella title, and I was in charge of the archaeological side of that department.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you explain briefly to the Trial Chamber what exactly archaeology is and how it's relevant to the exhumation of mass graves?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Well, archaeology is essentially the examination of the earth, of soils, for past relics, either for human remains or for artefacts, and these are then excavated and interpreted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: You started work for the ICTY in 1997; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Did you have any prior experience in exhuming mass graves?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes. In 1990 I was asked by the Attorney General of the Commonwealth government in Australia to go to the Ukraine, which was then part of the Soviet Union, to investigate three mass graves of Jews who had been murdered in 1942. There were three graves, and I was working there in 1990 and 1991 and made reports back to the Australian government on the existence of these graves, which contained something like 800 bodies between the three of them, and that material went to court. The reason why an Australian would be going over there was that there were three men in Adelaide, in South Australia, of whom it was said that they had participated in Nazi killings in the Ukraine in 1942 and had then emigrated to Australia after the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, when you were at the ICTY you worked with forensic anthropologists or in co-ordination with forensic anthropologists and pathologists. Can you briefly describe to the Chamber what those jobs do and how their work relates to yours as an archaeologist?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: The anthropologists that I had on my team, on my excavation team, were also experienced in archaeology. The reason for having them there is that they know their human bones inside-out and are therefore able to follow in muddy deposits. They're able to follow the way in which a body is disposed. There were also anthropologists at the morgue, which was not part of my operation, who were doing an analysis of the remains. But the anthropologists I had working with me were there because of their knowledge of the human body and skeleton and, because of this knowledge, were able to retrieve the bodies in a more complete and undamaged way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And what about the pathologists?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: No, we had no pathologists on the team.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: But at the morgue --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: -- you know, how -- how did their job relate to yours as part of the process of exhuming and analysing the remains?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Well, the process that was set up was that the morgue was in Visoko, which is close to -- close to Sarajevo, and we would periodically send the bodies that we had exhumed in chiller vans down to the morgue in Visoko. And there standard analyses were done of the biological profiles of the individuals, their age, sex, cause and manner of death, and that was done by anthropologists and pathologists but they were not part of my team. So the operation was divided into the exhumation team, of which I was in charge, and the anthropologists and pathologists at the morgue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you. The last exhumation you did for the ICTY was in 2000; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes. It would have been September/October 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Have you participated in any exhumations since then?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Not with ICTY, but I have participated in the exhumation of World War I Australian -- mostly Australian but some British soldiers who were killed in the First World War at a place called Fromelles in north-east France, and I was the senior forensic advisor to the Oxford archaeology team that had the contract to do this work, that is, to recover the bodies and to recover the uniforms and artefacts associated with the bodies which had been buried by the Germans after a disastrous battle. And then they were analysed on -- on the spot, DNA samples taken. And so, yes, I was the senior advisor for that project, but I didn't have an executive role.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you. Was there anything of significance or of interest about the disposition of those bodies?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: The bodies were collected, I'm not sure, two or three days after the battle, and they were in various disarranged -- the bodies were disarranged because many had been killed by shell blast, and the Germans buried them - it was a Bavarian regiment, in fact - the Germans buried them respectfully, side by side, alternately heads to the west and heads to the east and in two rows separated by a small quantity of soil, and altogether there were five graves that were full and contained 250 soldiers buried in their uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Were any of the people worked for you in Bosnia involved in that particular exhumation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes. The two graves were excavated at one time, and two of the people who had worked for me in Bosnia over a period of some weeks or months, one -- Oxford archaeology is a very experienced consulting firm in the UK, but they did not have experts in mass graves so they employed two people to be in charge of the excavations of each grave as it was done. Another person, Caroline Barker, who worked for me and was in charge of the anthropology at the anthropological laboratory at Fromelles, a -- the forensic photographer who took the photographs that are in my reports was the photographer for that project. So, yes, the people who worked for me in Bosnia went on to their own careers, but they were -- were captured, as it were, for the work at Fromelles, four of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one last very brief question about your background. We can see on your CV at the top it's Richard Wright AM, and this is different from your previous CVs. Can you explain very briefly what the AM means?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yeah, very briefly, I was made a member of the order of Australia in the Queen's honours list in May and it stands for Member of the Order of Australia, and that was awarded to me for my work in forensic archaeology, among other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you. Turning now to your work for the ICTY. You wrote two reports: "Exhumations in Eastern Bosnia in 1998" and "Excavations and Exhumations at Kozluk in 1999." Do you recall testifying about those two reports in the Krstic trial?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Have you had an opportunity to review your testimony in the Krstic trial?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And I understand you have one correction to that testimony. At transcript page 3633, at lines 19 and 21, there are two references to the word "objectives." That should read "objects"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. The context of what I was saying was that archaeologists specialise in recovering objects from the soil but that got written down as objectives.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, can you confirm that with that correction, the transcript of your testimony in Krstic, it accurately reflects your evidence in that case?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And if you were asked the same questions on the same topics today, would you give the same answers?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like to tender the Krstic testimony, which is 65 ter number 03227.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You are minded to tender Dr. Wright's CV as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Yes, my apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll admit that first.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. 65 ter number 03452 will be Exhibit P3998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And Professor Wright's testimony in Krstic will be admitted as Exhibit P3999.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd also like to tender at this point the associated exhibits and also the two reports that I mentioned. The first report, "Exhumations in Eastern Bosnia in 1998," is 65 ter number 2496; and the second report, "Excavations and Exhumations at Kozluk in 1999," is 65 ter number 2495.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Those two reports will be admitted as Exhibit 4000 and Exhibit P4001.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I'd now like to read a summary of Professor Wright's testimony in the Krstic case. Professor Wright started work for the ICTY in 1997. In 1998 he led the exhumations at the mass grave-sites at the Red Dam; Cancari Road 3; Cancari Road 12; Hodzici Road 3, 4, and 5; Liplje 2; and Zeleni Jadar 5. In 1999 he exhumed a primary mass grave at Kozluk. And at the time of his testimony in the Krstic case he was working at sites in Prijedor. Professor Wright described how an excavation would start, with him being taken by ICTY investigators to a suspected mass grave-site. It was then his job to find the actual location of the grave within that suspect area. First the site was checked for mines and booby-traps and a surveying team was set up to record the content -- sorry, to record the grave and its contents. A backhoe would then be used to scrape off the surface of the soil until Professor Wright was satisfied that the complete outline of the grave had been uncovered. Each of the bodies within the grave were surveyed with a three-dimensional recording system, and each body or body part was assigned a unique number and photograph. Where a virtually complete body was removed, the experts also filled out a form called a "body sheet" which described the properties of the body. Once the bodies and body parts had been exhumed, they were sent to the morgue for anthropological and pathological analysis. The details of the eight graves exhumed by Professor Wright in 1998 are as follows: The first site, known as the Red Dam, was a large primary grave dug into a dam wall made of limestone blocks. It had been robbed and contained no complete bodies. However, it contained many highly fragmented human remains, which according to the morgue accounted for a minimum number of 46 individuals. The remaining seven sites he exhumed that year - Cancari Road 3; Cancari Road 12; Hodzici Road 3, 4, and 5; Zeleni Jadar 5; and Liplje 2 - were all secondary graves. He concluded that the Liplje 2 secondary grave was connected to the Red Dam primary grave based on the presence of angular non-naturally occurring limestone blocks at both sites. In 1998, Professor Wright also probed an additional 21 sites that proved to be graves. He estimated that those 21 sites contained an additional 2.571 bodies. In 1999, Professor Wright exhumed a partially robbed primary mass grave-site at Kozluk. He concluded that this site was linked to the Cancari 3 secondary grave he had exhumed the previous year based on the presence of fragments of green glass present throughout both sites. He also concluded that the Kozluk site was an execution site as well as a burial site where some individuals had been simply covered with soil and left undisturbed. This conclusion was based on the lack of any disturbance to the limbs of those bodies and the recovery of bullets embedded in the clay underneath the bodies. Professor Wright observed that 42 per cent of the 280 individuals at the Kozluk site had their hands tied behind their back, while 16 per cent of the bodies were blindfolded. Professor Wright also noted that he saw only civilian clothing in the graves he exhumed in 1998 and 1999. I now have some additional questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Professor, you've spoken about primary and secondary graves in your prior testimony. Can you define for us what these are?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes. I think before doing that I need to also introduce a first category which is an execution site. A primary grave is where the bodies from an execution site are first buried. That in many cases, one might imagine, was the end of the matter, but these graves were dug up in most cases and the bodies were taken away to secondary graves. And so we distinguish between primary graves, the place of initial disposal, and secondary graves, which are the places to which the bodies were taken from the primary graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: In your reports you use the term "rob" to describe the process of removal from a primary to a secondary grave. Can you explain in a little bit more detail what you mean by this tern "rob"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes, the word "rob" or "robbed" is commonly used in archaeology to mean that when you excavate a site you see areas where things have been taken away. It may seem to -- in common usage that I'm talking about some type of a criminal act, but the word is used not necessarily to mean that. And there's a section in the Oxford English Dictionary devoted to the archaeological -- special archaeological use of the word robbed. So when I was using that term, I was using it as an archaeologist.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you to -- if you can, to give us an example of what you've been talking about, an execution primary grave and secondary grave. Can you tell us using the Kozluk site as an example about this process? Can you tell us how you first came to learn of the site at Kozluk?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: In 1998, we were excavating at a site called Cancari Road 3, and as the excavator was marking out the limits of the grave, that is, the machine, the machine, the backhoe, if you like, as it was marking out the boundaries of the grave, we saw hundreds if not thousands of pieces of broken green glass, and they were all of the same type of glass, from bottles, many of which had still got their crown seals on them even though they were broken, and we found a pile of labels, maybe 3- or 400 labels, which mentioned the Vitinka bottling factory at Kozluk. Now, this site was in a fairly desolate part of -- Cancari Road 3 was in an a fairly desolate part of Bosnia and there was no settlement around it, so I concluded that these bodies had been brought, together with the broken glass, from a primary site or an execution site, I didn't know which, but primary grave or an execution site that was at a place where the bottling factory dumped its broken bottles. So I got in touch with ICTY about this. And initially they were unaware of such an execution site or a primary grave in that area, but they immediately came down and we went to -- but we went behind the bottling factory and we found an area of -- by the Drina River that was grossly disturbed, and I think a couple of legs or it was a leg and an arm lying out below what looked like a loading ramp for trucks to pull up against. We hadn't found a grave by then, and in -- sorry, end of 1998, but in 1999 my team went back there and we found the primary grave which had been robbed and from which I conclude the bodies that were at Cancari 3 had been taken. They'd been taken from Kozluk to Cancari 3 transferring the evidence of the bottles and the labels, and Cancari 3 was certainly a secondary grave by the standards of the incompleteness of many of the bodies which had come apart in the -- while they were transferred.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to show you a few photos of this site and get you to explain them to us.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Can I ask which site?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Kozluk.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: 65 ter number 2495. Page 27 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I believe it's 2495.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is this what we admitted as one of his expert report?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Correct, Mr. President. If we can go to the next page in B/C/S so we can get the description.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. Professor, starting with the top photo, photo number 4, can you tell us what we're looking at here?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes. We're at -- we're at the site --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. If the Defence is okay, we can collapse the B/C/S and can zoom in to the picture. Would that be okay, Mr. Karadzic? Yes, we'll do that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the area of the Kozluk site that we called KK2. It's a distinct area from the main mass of bodies. But the reason why this was seen as important by us is that here you're looking down from some high ground onto a flat surface on which these bodies lie, and we found many of them visibly, that we then analysed them, visibly had gunshot wounds, and they -- and bullets were embedded up to about 10 centimetres -- I seem to have done some damage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Mitchell, would you -- would you like the doctor to mark on the picture?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. That might be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you wait a second until our usher could assist you. Yes, you can mark it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This is the flat surface here. And here are the bodies, obviously, lying down. Many of them had their hands tied behind their backs and/or were blindfolded, but I can't remember the numbers. But we found bullets embedded in the soil underneath these bodies down to a depth of 10 centimetres. These bodies were then covered up with soil after they had been -- died there, and later an attempt was made, not by us but previously, to recover the bodies, and you're beginning to see here an old trench that cut through the edge of these bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If we can scroll down and have a look at photograph 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do we need to preserve this one? Or we can --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: It's all the same page, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, I wanted -- I wanted to ask you whether you wanted to keep doctor's marking on this picture. At this moment it won't be necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Yeah, not yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we can -- yes, we can move on then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can scroll down to the next photo, photo number 5.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You would want me to talk now?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Yeah. You said we could see the edges of a trench.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Would you like the doctor to mark it again?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the surface we were looking at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh, no, just -- could you wait. Probably you need to push some pencil click first. Could you wait till assisted by our -- by our usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the flat surface that I was talking about previously. If it will help the proceedings, I can point but not touch.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If you can just, yeah, describe it to us.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes, okay. Well, we can see at the top of the photograph the same flat surface and the bodies lying on the flat surface. And right across the picture is a trench which, as you can see on the edges here, has -- has cut -- hmm. Anyway, the -- there is a cut right across the bodies that's taken away the leg of one of them, and this is done by an excavator with teeth. And the excavator that dug this trench and took away we don't know what but presumably some bodies, some from the edge here, this -- these marks are left by the excavator, because it compresses the soil in such a manner that when looser soil is thrown over the top the actual compressed grooves of the teeth are not obliterated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: And the archaeologists just take out the soft material. So my interpretation of this is that there was [Realtime transcript read in error "wasn't"] an execution there and that the attempt was made then to recover the bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think we can zoom in further at those parts. Yes. Once again. Further. Further, yes. We can see a bit clearer. Is this what you're -- what you're referring to, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I'm referring to the two critical parts of this photograph, are -- at the top, are undisturbed bodies. On the edge, some limbs have been taken away. And on the bottom you see the trench that cut through the mass of bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can we please go to page 30 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And just looking at the top photo, which is photo number 9, is that the green glass that you were talking about, Professor?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes. At the top of the screen you can see the green glass of which we have removed for sending down to the morgue many -- many bodies. In fact, at this particular area of the site, which is KK3, we found some 280 complete bodies, and these are the ones that are left down the slope, and that is the green glass.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Was it part of your protocol to keep the artefacts that were recovered from a site?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: In general, yes. And certainly any artefacts that were -- would bear on the cause and manner of death and the identification of the individuals. But an exception made at Kozluk and at Cancari 3 was that we did not collect all the glass because we considered it as background waste material that didn't bear on the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Professor, can I just clarify something in the transcript at page 15, line 13. It says my interpretation of this site is there wasn't an execution there. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: No. There was an execution there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If we can now scroll down to look at photo number 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Now, in your report at page 13 you estimated that there were some 16 per cent of the bodies had blindfolds and 43 per cent, or 124 bodies, had ligatures. Now, using this particular photo as an example, can you explain to us how you interpreted an artefact as a ligature or as a blindfold?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: I'm afraid of touching the screen, and I really do need to mark at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me just explain the layout of this body. Here is a head with hair. Here are the shoulder blades. And the -- and here are the ribs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you for your patience. Another way we can do it is put that picture on the ELMO and then doctor can point to the picture. We seem to have some problem with the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: That's fine with me, Mr. President. I don't have a colour version of that photo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't we use the -- your report, even in black and white.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I don't mean to interrupt. I just wonder if this is a problem that can be fixed if we need a five-minute break. I think it would be worth it so that the expert can mark as necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I agree. But before we take a break, short break: Mr. Tieger, we are seized of the motion from the Defence to either postpone or -- postpone/adjourn Mr. Jean-Rene Ruez's testimony or order him to testify live. Can -- when do you think you can give your response to this?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'll get back to the Court. I gather that's a request for a response as expedited as possible, and I'll report back on what we can manage as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So I'd like to hear from you before the end of business tomorrow. Thank you. Then we'll take a break for five minutes. So if you could tell us when it's ready. --- Break taken at 9.39 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you for your patience, Doctor. Let's, continue, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. We should be -- should be up and running, Professor. The question was: How do you interpret an artefact as a ligature or a blindfold?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes. I was, before the screen failed, I was pointing to the layout of this body. Here is the hair. We seem to have the same troubles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just wait. Wait a minute.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here is the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What am I doing wrong? Or is the machine wrong?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just -- could you wait till ... yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Sir, can we go down. It's the bottom photo we're looking at.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President. We do have colour copies here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't understand this. Let's put the colour copy on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now it's working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh, it is work-- now it works. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The head, the hair, the shoulder blades, the spine. And here we see the two arms meeting behind the back, and there is this cloth tied round the arms. This is the cloth holding them together behind the back. And this individual, although we're looking at the back of the skull and it's a bit obscured, but this is the blindfold here. So I would interpret those bits of cloth as not background waste from a rubbish dump but as so intimately related to the body that they are artefacts that must be recovered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you kindly, Doctor, put your -- put the date and your signature at the right bottom of the picture. Today is 1st of December.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. This page will be admitted as separate exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P4002, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I please go to page 32 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And just briefly, Professor, once this comes up I want to ask you if you recall what material the ligatures were made of at this site, whether they were made of the same material or something different.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: I can't answer that question as to whether they were all made of the same material. It wasn't something that was within my brief. But I seem to -- at Kozluk, most of the ligatures, I think all of them that are in that picture, are of cloth, but they were in -- except for these specially taken illustrations for our records, in general we were not analysing the nature of the material.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can we go back to page 29 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And you said earlier, Professor, that you interpreted that previous picture as a ligature because both hands were tied behind the back. How did you interpret this one as a ligature when it's only around one wrist?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If we can maybe zoom in photo number 8.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes. In the case of this individual, the ligature is around this arm, then there's a knot, and then there's a loop of cloth in this area, and I concluded that this individual had broken loose in his left arm from the ligature but had not broken loose on his right arm. So he's carried with the -- with it, with his right arm, the loop from which he's broken loose.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can I tender that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Professor, if you could write your initials and the date.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P4003.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Professor, I want to move to a different area now, and just a few questions about who you reported to at the ICTY during these exhumations. Can you tell us who you reported to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes. I -- in -- in terms of the structure of ICTY as it was then, I reported to the Chief of Operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Did the Chief of Operations direct you how to do your professional work at these sites?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: No. The Chief of Operations was very rarely at the sites but did make visits.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. What about the investigators who came to the site; did they direct your work, issue instructions on how to do the work?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: No, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I have a few questions about the protocols that you had in place at the site as well. Who developed these protocols?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: I developed them together with my team, and you're referring to a document which has a series of paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Is it possible to show one on the screen so that I know --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter 2495. That's the Kozluk report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And it should be around page 6, starting with the heading "Exhumation Procedures."

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay, so these are the protocols that you developed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes. And these were printed and given to each member of the team, and I took each member of the team through the protocols to explain what they mean. Essentially they describe who's responsible for doing what during the exhumation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And were these protocols put in place at all the Srebrenica-related sites and the three Prijedor sites that you exhumed at Redak, Pasinac cemetery, and Kevljani?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes, they were, and they were essentially the same for each site but with some differences that depended on the nature of the site. But they were -- they are essentially the same in 1997 -- sorry, in 1998, 1999, and 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And have these protocols received peer recognition or been followed at other sites other than the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: They were certainly used. They're not published. The principles behind them were incorporated into a book, "The Scientific Investigation of Mass Graves," which was published by Dr. Cox, and to which people who worked for me contributed. And I can see the influence of these protocols which were developed, and not by me personally but in conjunction with my team of surveyors, photographers, and scene-of-crime officers. Yes, they do have -- have had some influence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. When we were talking about Kozluk, I asked you about whether you preserved the green glass and you said no. Was there any other occasion where you didn't preserve an artefact at a site?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes. At the -- at the Red Dam that you've referred to, which we worked on in April maybe to May 1998, there were no complete bodies. There were isolated bones. And in the filling of the -- the refilling of that grave at the Red Dam, there were isolated pieces of clothing that were not associated with any bones and which were industrially manufactured clothing that would not have led to the identification of individuals, and so they were put back -- some of those were put back in the grave. But what was retained were things like knitted sweaters which somebody might recognise as their own handiwork. That is the only occasion on which I discarded artefacts, but that was after photography.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, just one question about the 21 sites that were probed in 1998, and you estimate that had these sites contained 2.571 bodies. Have you subsequently come into any information that would cause you to revise that estimation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes. If I -- if I could just expand on that a bit. We -- we had -- I had information from the morgue of -- about the number of bodies in seven of the secondary graves that we had excavated. There were 21 graves that we had probed, and the principles of probing were to define the outline of the grave and show there were more than two individuals in the grave but not exhume them, and I did some calculations, which are estimates, and came up with that number that you mentioned. More particularly, I came up with an average number, which I think was about 122 in each grave. So I put in my report that if you accept certain assumptions there, then -- I'm bad on remembering numbers. If I could consult my notes, Mr. President on this. Could I consult my notes on the numbers that I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By all means, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. From the -- in the report on the 1998 season, where we had seven secondary graves and I was asked to estimate how many bodies there might be in the 21, I came up, as you said, with an estimate of 2.571, which was an average of 120 -- based on the average of 122.4 bodies that we actually found. I was concerned that my estimate -- whether -- were my estimates widely out, so I have kept up with people who have worked since on the exhumation of these probed secondary graves that I didn't exhume, and in particular Mr. Jon Sterenberg who worked for ICMP told me of the number of individuals in ten of those probed graves and the -- that was an average of greater than 151, which meant that my estimate back in -- in 1999 was an underestimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: I also consulted a much later report by Dusan Janc, which is an official ICTY document, and he had information at that point, that was last year, of the number of individuals in 19 of the 21 probed graves and they had an average of 137.6. So, say, 138 bodies actually recovered. So my estimates in that report you're referring to were a slight underestimate. There were more bodies in those probed graves than I had estimated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Mitchell. Do you have any problem, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I think it's colder than it should be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Just to clarify: Professor, you were shown the report by Dusan Janc when you came here for your testimony in the Tolimir case last year?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: I can't remember whether I was shown it before or afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I want to move to a different area now, which is your exhumation at the Glogova 1 site.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And if I can bring up 65 ter 2504.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And just while that's coming up: Professor, were the same protocols in place at this site that were in place at your 1998 and 1999 excavations?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Not the same in the sense of identical, but the principles were the same, yes. I think by 2000 we decided we would not -- in 1999 at Kozluk where there were some hundreds if not thousands of shell cases from bullets, we decided we would not survey each one. We did survey each one, but we didn't photograph each one, as we would have done before. So that's explicit in our 2000 -- protocols for the year 2000, but if there's artefacts like AK-47 shell cases exceeds a certain number, we won't photograph every one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: But that's the sort of difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And is this the report that you wrote on that exhumation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can we please go to page 26 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can you describe to us what we're looking at in this photo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Maybe we can blow it up.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think we can safely collapse the B/C/S part.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We're looking at -- at the site which is called Glogova 1. I hardly dare touch the screen, but I will risk it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Just -- just wait one moment, Professor.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes. This is essentially the area of Glogova 1, which I excavated. And over the road here is Glogova 2, which I was not responsible for that excavation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And just -- just to orient us, the road that we can see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you just orient us, the road that we see running along the top half of the picture?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes. Essentially it's running on the left to Kravica and the warehouse, which I think is about 6 kilometres, and to the right this main road is running to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: And then there is a side road here which is a track, which leads up to the two Glogova sites.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you please put your initials and date that.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If that can be admitted, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Exhibit P4004.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If we can go to page 28 next.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Now, this is a complex site, Professor, so if -- when the next image comes up, if you can just briefly describe the site and the various sub-graves within it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Actually, maybe page 29 may be better.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: So there are six separate deposits here; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: There are six separate surviving deposits. The -- I divide the site into two areas. There is this area that I'm drawing a red line around, which I'll mark as 1, and then there are three discrete small graves on the left-hand side of the picture marked as grave E, K, and L. This area to the right, which I've labelled 1, was probably once a very much large area of mass graves, and these marks on -- that we have put on and called grave H, grave F, and grave C, are surviving patches of body -- of bodies. It -- from a grave that was robbed in October 1995. And so this is what was left behind that we found. On the left are graves that were not disturbed in October 1995 and so they are intact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And how do you know that these graves were robbed in October 1995?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Because we see signs of excavators having cut through the bodies, and there are these dismembered limbs left behind after a -- after an attempt was made to remove the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And what about the specific time period that you gave, October 1995; how did you conclude that that's when the robbing occurred?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: I was shown aerial images which are included in my report which allows me to see first of all when the original burials were made, which was in July 1995. That's all the burials were made.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: And then in October 1995, these aerial images show the disturbance of the area I've marked 1? And there's -- one of the aerial images shows a large excavator working in this area, mechanical excavator working in this area, which I'll call 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. If you can initial and date that.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Professor, did you include that -- those aerial images you saw at the time into your report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Where can we see them, Mr. Mitchell? We'll mark -- we'll admit this as Exhibit P4005. Do you have your report in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I do, Mr. President. I think it's, Mr. President, at page 27. It's an aerial image dated the 27th of July for three -- sorry, four aerial images, 5th of July, 17th of July, 27th of July, and then 30th of October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: After having kept this image, we'll move to page 27 to take a brief look. I think it's in front of you at the monitor, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could give us some brief explanation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. This is the area which we investigated. And on the 5th of July, in this aerial photograph, it's an undisturbed area. On the 17th of July, this photograph to the right, there's a lot of disturbed soil showing up. We recognised this in photograph after photograph. You can't dig graves without disturbing soil. And this area here is the area within which burials were made. These letters in blue are the labels we gave to patches of surviving bodies for our own notes, and they remain unchanged in all of the four photographs. The -- on the 27th of July you can see that the area is smoothed over. And this area down at the bottom of the picture, K and L, has got graves which were not there on the 17th of July, this area which I'll mark as 2, in both cases on the 17th of July it actually has one of the graves, but the -- the -- there are two graves here which were -- there are two graves here which appear after, that is E and L. And the disturbance of the site that took place on the 30th of October, where you can see big areas of new disturbed soil which are not present here, this type of robbing did not extend to these graves down here, K, E, and L. The photograph of the excavator at work was not available to me when I wrote this report, and so it's not included in the report, the aerial image.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can you initial that and date it, Professor.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Exhibit P4006. Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Were you able to establish any links between this grave at Glogova 1 and a secondary grave-site?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes. Rather in the same way as the link between Cancari Road 3 and Kozluk, we in fact found one of the secondary graves for the Glogova site before we found the primary grave. The secondary grave we found in 1998, at the end of the season, is Zeleni Jadar 5. And Zeleni Jadar 5 had certain peculiar properties compared with the other graves we had dug. For instance, there were a lot of motorcar parts, barbed wire, hay. This was mixed up with the bodies. And even an unripe apple, which, although it might seem of little consequence, at least allows one to judge approximately the season at which these bodies were buried. Then in 2000 when we excavated the Glogova site, we consistently found -- well, there are orchards, trees overhanging the graves, and we were finding motorcar parts, parts of buildings, barbed wire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Did you find hay Glogova 1?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: We found hay. We found hay in Glogova 1. There's a picture in my report of the hay. And we found, more particularly and which was of great interest to the investigators, we were finding parts of -- broken-off parts of what was clearly a building. And Mr. Mike Hedley, who was a British police officer, was commissioned to write a report on the relationship between these bits of building that we were finding at Glogova with the Kravica warehouse. And I personally went down there and saw the Kravica warehouse, that the door had been -- that the arch above the door had been broken. And in the graves at Glogova 1 we were able to assemble virtually the complete door from -- which we recovered from various parts of the site mixed in with the bodies, the frame, the joists, the door itself, pieces of cement which were painted white and some painted red, and polystyrene which was used. You could see at the warehouse itself polystyrene was used as an insulator between the cement panels that formed the wall. But I didn't do an analysis of that material. I formed an impression. But there is a separate analysis done.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. There's one other artefact, or type of artefact, that you describe in that grave, which is shrapnel- and grenade-related artefacts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If we can go to page 37 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If you can just explain what it is that we're looking at in these five photographs, starting with the one at the top of the page, 56763_15?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes. There we're looking at a pellet of metal embedded in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't you zoom in, just for the first picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here we're looking at a very shattered skull. And embedded in the skull is this pellet. And the unexploded ordnance officer that we had with us explained, for our own safety, explained to me that this is a pellet from a grenade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Do we need to save this page now or scroll down and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't we --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: We can save it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: You can initial and date it, Professor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Exhibit P4007.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And if we can scroll down and look at the next two photos down on that page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And, Professor, if you can just describe what we're looking at in these two photos.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Well -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: We're looking at some flesh, I don't know what, maybe the shoulder, the skin. And the one on the left is a general photograph and the one on the right is a close-up of the same effect, but here a piece of metal embedded in the flesh.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Just for the record -- sorry. Just for the record, we're looking at photo 56715_04a. And if we can just scroll across so I can get the number of the second one. If we can save that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Professor, if you can initial and date that.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Just for the record, the second photo we were looking at was 56715_05a. And now if we can scroll down and look at the bottom two photos on that page, which are 56726_25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The previous one was admitted as Exhibit P4008; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And the second photo we're looking at here on the right is 56757_24. And again, Professor, if you can just explain what it is we're looking at here.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Here we're looking at a piece of bent metal which is found with the bodies. And I was told again by the unexploded ordnance officer that this is the fly-off, I believe that's the name, the fly-off lever of a grenade which is lifted and causes the grenade to explode. And the one on the left is a second one of those but not bent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. If I can now go to page 17 in e-court, 17 in the English, 16 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Professor, that's page 16 in your hard copy, if you'd like to take a look.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Do you want me to initial it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Yes, please. No, you haven't marked it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, you don't have to because you didn't mark anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. Now, at this part of your report you talk about how the bodies in this site are -- you describe them as unusually fragmented, and you conclude that some of this is due to blast injuries as well as the burial process itself. Can you just briefly expand on this conclusion.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Well, the bones were more broken up within the clothing than at any of the other sites we examined, and the association with the bodies of grenades and flesh -- and metal embedded in the flesh led me to conclude that we were looking at blast damage. But, but, these bodies go to the morgue. These are the impressions -- contingency impressions that I form at the site, but I have no doubt that these bodies suffered blast damage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What paragraph are we looking at on this page?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: That's the very bottom of the page. My apologies. It's over on page 16, the paragraph that starts with "In the light of this unusual fragmentation, I consider it significant that Glogova 1 is the only primary site where I have found remains of explosive devices in the form of grenades and shrapnel."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Where is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh, yes. In -- yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. I want to take you to one last area and that's a video --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to tender doctor's report it testify?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. You are not tendering his interim report, are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Exhibit -- the 65 ter 2504 will be admitted as Exhibit P4009. I take it there's no opposition.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, the only thing I have left is some video footage of about 10 minutes, but with breaks and explanations it could be 20, 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We will take a break in a few minutes. But before that shall we deal with associated exhibits --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- with this transcript you tender. Two -- just, first question is: Two expert reports which have been already tendered are listed as one -- as one of those associated exhibits, but we're not minder to tender them separately?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 65 ter number 20576. And, before that, 65 ter 2494. Can we upload it? This is just one-page diagram. utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I have looked. I don't believe that we have the original in colour, but Professor Wright does, so we may be able to rescan --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Professor, we're going to look now at a video of the Cancari 12 site that you exhumed in 1998. But before we start, I just wonder if you could give the Trial Chamber a bit of background about this site. Just describe where it is and some of the general properties.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes. The Cancari 12 site was the first site that we excavated that was a secondary grave in 1998. It's at one extreme end of what we call the Cancari Road, that is, the end of the Cancari Road that's furthest away from the Drina River. It was shown to us by -- or, rather, we were taken to it by investigators, and I had to see whether it was feasible to excavate the site and we were able to get all our transport in and all the necessary buildings that would have to go up to do the work, and, well, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. That might be an appropriate point to start the film. And I'll -- rather than talking during the footage, we'll just watch a bit and then I'll stop and get you to explain what it is that we've just seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: So if we can start.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. If we can stop there. The time is 00:25 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And if you can describe what we just saw in that image, Professor.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes, what we saw in that image was the grave before any excavation started. And the people responsible for the surveying that was going to take place were -- were -- were setting up their equipment, establishing a baseline and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If we can start again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If we can just stop there. That's 01:05 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And if you can describe this.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: What we've seen there is the initial search for the boundaries of the grave. The archaeological principle is that you find the grave outlines before you disturb any of the bodies. And how do you find the grave outlines? Well, excavation in this sort of soil brings up mineralised material from down below and mixes it up with the organic material on top that this backhoe that you saw in the film is scraping through. So when the grave is refilled, there's a mottled soil in the filling of the grave, it contains top-soil and subsoil, and the boundary of the grave therefore can show up when you have a decent scrape across the surface, a nice smooth scrape. And that's what this backhoe is doing, searching for the boundaries of the grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Sir, what are the specific things that are being looked for, the specific signs? Like, is there change in texture of the soil, colour of the soil? Like, what are the things that -- the specific indicia that they're looking for?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Well, exactly as I've described. Because a grave is dug through a developed soil profile, it mixes it all up. And so the archaeologists are looking, where this excavator is working, for a change in texture or colour and then tracking that to see if it makes sense in terms of the outline of a grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If we can keep going.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. If I can just stop there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Two questions. First, what -- what are the orange flags that we saw you -- or we saw being put in place a few seconds ago?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: The orange flags are temporary markers of what the archaeologist thinks is the boundary of the grave as it's being developed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. And second: Can you explain the colour of the soil here, what we're looking at, at this particular shot?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And I'll just -- the time we stopped the video at is 01 minutes and 47 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The natural colour of the soil is black at the organic horizon at the top and then it changes to a reddish colour and then it changes to a much paler colour with a natural deposit. When bodies have been put into a grave and the grave has been refilled, the soil around the bodies changes colour. This is because the ferric oxide in the soil, which -- if you'd like to think of it as rust, the ferric oxide in the soil is changed by the bacteria that putrefy the bodies. This is an -- these are anaerobic bacteria, and the world over this is a phenomenon that's observed, where iron is in the soil. The -- an oxygen atom from the ferric oxide is taken by these bacteria to keep them alive and the soil changes to the ferrous state because of the loss of that oxygen molecule. So this a -- these blueish-green soils is a very useful indicator that bodies, not necessarily human bodies, but organic bodies have been in -- been in that spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can we restart.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. If I can just stop there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What are we -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Sorry, yeah, what stage of the process are we at here now?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Well, the previous stage that we saw, people with picks and trowels, were not digging up bodies but they were following on from the mechanical excavator by using picks, mattocks, and trowels to define the grave precisely. Then the next step is to put in a sounding within the area of the -- of what is thought to be the grave to see if there are indeed bodies in the grave, and so this is the sounding that's put in to check that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And that's at 2 minutes and 49 seconds. And if we can start again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Stop there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: We can see a dig trench now. Can you explain what stage of the process the excavation is at now?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Well, once the sounding that we saw in the previous -- the previous part of the video, once the sounding is established that there are bodies, then the filling of the grave above those bodies has to be removed. And if there's danger of flooding of the grave during the course of work, a sump is put in to catch the water by the side. So you're seeing a mixture of the removal of the filling of the grave down to the level of the bodies and the digging of a deeper trench along the side which would catch the water if it should -- there should be torrential rain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Now, we saw the backhoe working at the start. We're now starting to see work being done by hand. How much of the excavation is done by hand from this point onwards?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: All the work around bodies is done by hand. The excavator is for the removal of -- the mechanical excavator is for the removal of material that is not containing bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. If we can start the video again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Stop there. Stop there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. What are we looking at here?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Well, we jumped forward several days from the previous point where you stopped the video, and the -- the side trench had been, as you notice, had put boards there, and the bodies were now being exposed. The -- and taken away in body bags to the chiller van where they were then taken to the morgue in Visoko. So there's a big gap in time between the two sets of shots.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: But this specifically, what's the machine that we're looking at in the centre of the shot?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And that shot is at 4 minutes and 22 seconds.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Now, this is a -- what we call a total station, a surveying instrument for measuring the -- for any particular artefact or point on a body, it measures the number of metres east, the number of metres north, and the elevation of the point in relation to our datum. And from that, then we can reconstruct in three dimensions the location of a particular artefact or particular body and generate stick figures to represent the human skeletons that were in the -- in the excavation. So this is the surveying instrument which allows us to reconstruct the three-dimensional patterns within the grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And you survey these 12 points on the body; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes. Then we were using 12 points on the body. We're using the head, the shoulders, the elbows, the wrists, the pelvis, the knees, and ankles, and from that it was possible to construct a three-dimensional map of the grave in stick figures. And then you can, on the computer, rotate those images so that you can see, perhaps, piles of bodies from the side. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. Can we start again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: We've stopped at 5 minutes and 2 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can you describe what -- what we see on the screen here, Professor?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes. Well, just as background, the Cancari 12 grave was a secondary grave, and the bodies had been removed from a site that I'm told is the Branjevo Farm. And in the course of removing the bodies from that primary grave at Branjevo Farm, many of them were broken up so that we had some isolated hands and limbs. I can't recall the details of this particular individual, but I know what we're looking at. We're looking at a hand and a knot of cloth in what would be the area of the wrist, so a ligature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And can we start again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. If we can just stop there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: What's the code that we're looking at there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: The code -- the C is obscured by the block of soil on the left, but that would be CR12 that designates the site, and the code A046 indicates that it's the 46th -- it's an artefact with the number 046. I don't know what the artefact is, I can't see, but these would be probably the ligature that we saw in the previous shot, but I'm not sure. And the -- these entries are then made into a log so that each of these items -- item A046 would be an item in the log that was kept for the site.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And just for the record, that was at 5 minutes and 31 seconds. And we can restart.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Just stop there. Six minutes, 22 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can you describe what this, the white object we see on the screen now?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes, this is one of the plastic body bags that we used, zipped from top to bottom -- or from all along the top, rather, I should say. And the label on it is CR12, and it's B095. I think it's a 9. And so that signifies that this bag is going to include a whole body. Now, the body may not be removable in its complete state so that bits may have to be removed bit by bit, but into that bag, that body bag, would have gone a body which was virtually complete. And then these body bags are transferred to the chiller van.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: How would the code for a body part be different?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: If that had been a body part, it would be BP092, BP standing for body part.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: We can restart.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can we stop there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: What's this, the sheet that we're looking at here?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: This is one of the body sheets. So when a body was complete or nearly complete, the person responsible for uncovering that body would fill out some summary details which would include the -- the -- the lay -- layout of the body, whether it showed any puncture marks, whether it was -- what kind of clothing it was wearing, any associate artefacts would be listed on; what is really a checklist to remind the excavator to make certain observations. And at the very bottom you see a schematic diagram of how the body was laid out, together with some notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And that was at 6 minutes and 40 seconds. And we can restart.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Just stop there. That's 7 minutes and 52 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Now, there's several parts going into a body bag here. Can you describe -- well, just describe what we're seeing.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes, earlier on we just saw for a flashing moment the label, which was a B label, so it's a body, but the body is being removed in bits and pieces, although these were together in the grave, and they're now being removed as bits and pieces and reassembled, as it were, in the body bag.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can we restart.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If we can just stop there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Where's this body being taken to now, Professor?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Well, that -- just at the beginning of the sequence you saw the excavators putting plastic bags over the hands, and they would also put them over the feet so the various parts of the hand don't fall off in transport. They stay together. And now the body is being taken to the chiller van on a stretcher.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And that was at 8 minutes and 38 seconds. And we can restart.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If we can just stop there. Nine minutes and 8 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can you describe what's going on here, Professor?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes, two things. The -- well, one -- one thing in this case. They are looking for wallets or any other form of identification, such as a necklace, which we could photograph. Not because it's the final study of any documents that might be found with this body but because we were afraid that documents would perish in the interval between their removal from the grave and their arrival at the morgue where they were studied in more detail by investigators. So it was our custom to see if there was a wallet in a pocket and, if so, to open it up, because when you open up a wallet you're normally seeing a primary identification document, and then that's photograph, and the wallet is then closed and put back. And minimum -- there's minimum -- there are two reasons why there's minimum decay from this point on. One is that the bag is sealed so there's little oxygen, and oxygen is very damaging to paper documents. And the second thing is that it's kept under cold conditions which again slows down the fungal and bacterial decay that would take place in documents. So they're looking for any document that would -- could be opened up and photographed, and then that could be recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: You probably can't give us an exact answer, but how -- how quickly would a piece of paper degrade after coming out of site like this? Is it hours or days or weeks?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: I don't know. We were not -- we had no -- apart from the general principles that it's bad for a document to be re-oxygenated, as it were, and being allowed to dry out in particular, we -- I don't know. This was a precaution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: We can restart.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And stop there. Ten minutes, 10 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Was that the chiller van that we just saw in the picture?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: It was. And you saw the scene-of-crime officers who were responsible for formally handing over the bodies and the artefacts doing that part of the job, putting them in the chiller van and closing the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And from there the bodies go to the morgue?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And that's where the anthropologists and the pathologists start their examination of the remains?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes. And the investigators would -- the investigators would start their examination of the artefacts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, it's now time for Mr. Karadzic to start his cross-examination. Just a second. I think this video is a part of the associated exhibit, but shall we give the number separately now.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's Exhibit P4027, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Excellencies, good afternoon to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Professor.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At the very outset I would like to say to you that I highly appreciate the impressive work that you did, and I would like to ask you for your understanding, namely the Defence has to establish which part of your work can be considered established beyond reasonable doubt in terms of criminal law, that is to say, what has actually been established or, on the other hand, what can be disputed or challenged.
