On the whole, this is an impressive body of work. I'm not attacking it in any way. I'm just saying that we should find out what it is that has been established, actually. Do you agree with that.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you something. At the very outset you said that you worked for the international criminal court. Am I right if I specify this by saying that you were engaged by the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes, I was, under contract.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you that because in our legal system there is an investigative judge who can be engaged and that judge has to be impartial, where someone working for the Office of the Prosecutor need not be. So who is your employer from the side of the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: I was answerable to the Chief of Operations of whom there were three different people during the time I worked in the four years. That was the person that I was answerable to, who had, I suppose, the right of hire and fire, the right to hire me or fire me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you say Chief of Operations, was he in charge of anything else or was it only these operations? What kind of a particular post is that? Can you help us with that? What did these operations include?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I don't know. I can't answer that. I was not employed within the whole system of ICTY, so I'm not familiar with the structure or the responsibilities of that person other than to provide my support for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The second sentence here in your introduction in Glogova 1, you say: "I was asked to identify and exhume graveyards -- or, rather, the graves of persons who were allegedly killed after the taking of Srebrenica." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we consider, then, that all the bodies that were accessible to you, that your team had exhumed, that is -- actually, that you established that these people died after the taking of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Can you clarify, please? Do you mean just at Glogova or are you talking about all these sites we've heard about today?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, is this the assignment that you were given for all the locations or only for Glogova?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: No. I asked the question because a lot of the work I did was not related to the Srebrenica case. I worked in Prijedor. But for the sites that we've heard about today, yes, it was my understanding that the ICTY believed that these were people who were killed after the fall of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My interest is in Eastern Bosnia, not Prijedor, what is part of this case. Professor, did you obtain any other information from someone? Were you informed about what it was that had been going on there and what you would be up against, as it were?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Do you mean what is -- what had -- what happened at Srebrenica and what I could expect to find? I'm not quite sure what the question means.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me put it in simple terms. The war started there in April 1992. The war went on all the way up until October 1995. Srebrenica was declared a safe haven, a protected area, in May 1993. Before July 1993, about 2.000 fighters lost their lives from Srebrenica only. And not only in Srebrenica itself, but as they were going out into Serb-held territory. Could you differentiate as to who had lost their lives before the take-over of Srebrenica and who lost their lives after the take-over of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: No. I -- I -- I don't see how I could have established that, and I can't answer your question there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. You have given an answer, and I'm not attacking your findings at all. You have done a great deal of work. Do you know that people were dying every day in that area? Serbs and Muslims were dying every day. Have you received that information at all?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Not in my official capacity as an independent investigator of the graves, no, but I have read newspapers and heard news about events. But I was not officially told very much about the background to the fall of Srebrenica. I was asked to investigate certain graves and to determine how the people -- how many people were in them, what the properties of these bodies were, what associated artefacts were, but I'm -- I'm not an expert in the history of the -- of the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let us put it simply, in simple terms. Professor, you stated on page 47, line 18, it was -- line 19, 20: "It was my understanding that the ICTY," I take it to be the OTP, "ICTY believed that these were people who were killed after the fall of Srebrenica." But it was not for you to establish that fact.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was for me to establish that fact, yes, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But, I mean, they were killed after the fall of Srebrenica or -- or may have been killed before the fall of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, I see what you mean. My understanding was that they had fallen -- that they had died after the fall of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But did you establish that fact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'd say my -- yes, I believe I established that fact, that they were people who had died after the fall of Srebrenica. I don't -- I didn't work -- I mean, I imagine the people who died before the fall of Srebrenica, say within Srebrenica itself, would have been buried there, but I didn't work around Srebrenica. We worked in areas to which bodies had been taken. Now, my understanding of the history is that people were taken away from Srebrenica, and all the people that I excavated were taken away from Srebrenica, and I don't think for that reason that they died before the fall of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So one -- was one of your mandates to establish the timing of the death of those bodies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I -- it would have been. Or I was asked to advise whether it was reasonable to think that these people had died after the fall of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, Mr. -- back to you, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you establish and did they show you graves -- or, rather, was it your obligation to investigate all the accessible mass graves?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: No, Mr. Karadzic. I was shown aerial images that the -- that had fresh patches of soil on them dating from October 1995, and I was shown photographs that, on my analysis, had about 28 of these patches of soil that appeared, you know, over a period of a couple of days in October 1995, and I went to all of these and decided which of them we could excavate in the season that was available, in the season that was available which was about six months. And so my advice was sought as to how many we could reasonably excavate in that time. It was not possible to excavate more than seven of those in that time. But as I said earlier in my testimony, we probed the other sites it showed on the aerial photographs to establish that they were -- that they had multiple human remains in them, but we didn't exhume them. So in answer to your question was it my obligation to investigate all the accessible mass graves, yes, to investigate, but not to excavate. Excavation was restricted to seven.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Which method did you apply, and in which way did you establish the time of death?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Well, we -- we -- we established that the watches that were worn by some of the individuals were consistent with the date of the executions, and that analysis is in my report. They're consistent. The -- we also found artefacts of a sort, which, again, are in my report, such as Dutch newspaper that was cut up into cigarette papers and was in the pockets of the victims. But the main way in which we established the age of those graves was that they -- that is, the secondary graves of the 1998 season, is that they do not appear before October 1995. We have images of the ground before October 1995 and then suddenly these graves appear. So that is the best way of determining the age of the graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The age of the graves. But the time of death is something different. That's not the age of the graves. How did you establish when a man had died?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: I was not able to establish when a man had died other than by the context of the artefacts that came out of the grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you trying to say that a watch would show the hour, day, month, and year of execution?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: The particular watches that I'm talking and which are in my report are Seiko mechanical or automatic watches that stop within 24 to 48 hours of the last movement of the watch. Now, I'm told that the executions took place on Friday, the 14th of July, and eight out of the ten watches that we found in the 1998 season showed a day and a date, that is, Saturday 15 or Sunday 16, which is consistent with the information I received about the date of executions. But apart from that, apart from that I have evidence of the age of the graves. But if I look at an individual, I can't tell you when that individual died, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, just -- if there's going to be more questions on the topic of watches, I think the report in question is -- it's -- it had 65 ter 2496, and it might be helpful to bring it up if there's going to be further questions on this. And it starts -- there's a section on this topic that starts at around page 28.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So all of these watches were automatic mechanical ones? There were no battery operated watches? Electronic ones?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: There were windup watches and there were electronic watches, but they do -- the windup watches do not show day and date in the window. I really believe at this stage I should have a picture of the watch -- of one of the watches to explain what I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it's the penultimate page of the first report. Exhibit P4000. Page 181. E-court page. Did you refer to this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I referred to this type of watch, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And this is not a windup watch; right? This is an electronic or an automatic mechanical watch. Oh, it says automatic, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes, it's an automatic mechanical watch that is self-winding but stops after no movement within 24 or 48 hours. And this watch is showing in its window the day Sab, which is either Italian or Spanish for Saturday, 15. And this is one of the watches that I'm talking about where eight out of ten were consistent with an execution on Thursday -- on Friday the 14th. And I argue in my report that the probabilities of eight out of ten watches showing these day/dates that are consistent with the supposed execution date is trillions to one. Some special event happened that made these watches stop, not at random, but in a pattern. Now, you asked about the electronic watches and the -- well, you asked about electronic watches, and they, of course, continued to go on until the battery runs out. So they are of no forensic use. Windup watches tend not to have the day/date window. They may show a day -- a date, but not a day. The power of these watches for forensic purpose lies in the fact that they show a day and a date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Of course we agree, don't we, that neither the month nor the year is displayed; right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: No. Neither the -- the year and the month aren't displayed. So they're not as good as they might be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, did you get any information about the customs involved or even legal regulations, namely that detainees in our country cannot have watches, money, IDs, that is to say that persons who are arrested or detained cannot have any valuables on them until they are proven innocent in a court of law?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: No, Mr. Karadzic. I'm completely unaware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you believe me if I were to say to you that our people of any religious background are very reluctant to take anything from a dead person, whereas anything can be taken off a living person?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: It's -- it's a custom that I would not disbelieve, but I don't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you informed that around those days, during the fall of Srebrenica and after the fall of Srebrenica, there was a great deal of fighting around Srebrenica and that many people lost their lives? On both sides.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: When you say "informed," I wasn't specifically briefed on this by officers of ICTY, but it's something that I have read about, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So was your task to establish who had lost their lives after the -- the fall of Srebrenica in an unlawful way, by execution, or just to establish how these person had lost their lives?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: No. My -- my specific task was to investigate these graves which, as I've said, in 1998 were the secondary graves that -- turned out to be secondary graves, and to collect together the sort of evidence that I've already given testimony on. It was -- obviously I could see that many of these people had gunshot wounds, but it wasn't my job to determine how they'd lost their lives. That was the responsibility of the anthropologists and the pathologists in the morgue to give an official statement. But I have seen, particularly in my Ukrainian work, hundreds of people who had been shot, and I know what gunshot wounds look like, so I formed an opinion that these people had lost their lives in a violent way, but it wasn't my job to establish how these persons lost their lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me ask you a general question. If you were to be given this very same task again in that same area, in view of this experience would you change anything in this other investigation that you'd carried out -- that you would carry out? Would you improve anything? Would you make things any different? Would you change anything?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: I would not change any of the major procedures that we used, which is the discovery of the grave with the least amount of damage to the bodies, the recovery of the bodies with records of surveying so that we could work out where they came from in the grave, the photography of each of the bodies and artefacts before they were moved. No, I wouldn't change any of those procedures, and they're ones that I continue to use, which were -- well, when I say "I continue to use," I mean which continue to be used at the excavation of soldiers at the Fromelles site that's already been mentioned from World War I. I wouldn't -- I wouldn't make major changes at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you change anything as a result of remarks or objections that were made on your final report, some of which you replied to and some of which you accepted? And what would those changes be that you would make when taking into account the objections that were made?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Well, I'm afraid I don't know what the remarks or objections that were made on my final report are. You'd have -- you'd have to specify what they were before I could answer that question. I mean, I don't know in which context these objections were made other than in my courtroom testimony in the previous three cases, of Krstic and the Popovic seven and Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I will try to narrow that down. Is it correct that Dr. Zoran Stankovic remarked that pursuant to Article 19 of the Additional Protocols to the Geneva Conventions, or some other document, each interested party has the right to participate or to have an observer during the inspection? And I think that you said that that perhaps was the case but that that was not your job, actually, to allow for this.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes. That is the answer I would give now. I was not responsible for the logistics and security of the work. I don't remember that particular question being asked of me. That would have been in the Krstic case, I imagine. But I -- it's still not my responsibility to determine who should be allowed or not allowed at the site.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, when you stated which personnel took part in the exhumation, you said that no citizen of former Yugoslavia took part in this examination work. Did any such citizen attend the work that was being carried out?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: No. That statement is correct. And, no citizen of the former Yugoslavia was allowed to come to the sites in the four years that I excavated. And the -- at night the sites were under armed guard to prevent anyone coming in. Had ICTY said to me that they wished me to admit such a person, I would have, of course, admitted them, but the general rule was that no citizen of the former Yugoslavia was allowed near the work. To the extent, for instance, at the Red Dam where we needed a heavier excavator, an owner driver, somebody who owned the heavier excavator and drove the excavator, was not allowed into the site to use it. Our engineer drove the vehicle. So it was a strict policy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I understood you correctly, this was not that was established by you. This was a ban that was articulated or placed by somebody else; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: It was a policy that was -- a ban, in English, has a particularly -- a particular meaning, but it was a policy that we were not to allow such people into the site, yes. And I had a project manager for the site who dealt with such matters. It was not for me to -- I was there strictly to do the forensic work, not to engage in policy discussions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not attacking you in any way. I just want to determine who violated the right of Republika Srpska pursuant to Article 19 of the Additional Protocols to be present and to take part in the exhumations. You were not the one responsible for that, but this right was violated, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: I'm not aware of the rights and so I can't comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that you did see and comment on the fact that you agreed with the objection of Dr. Zoran Stankovic, a forensics expert from Belgrade, that perhaps that was so but that that was not your job. So we will find that reference and we will establish that in a different way. So you did allow for the possibility that this article of the Additional Protocols does exist?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The doctor said he is not aware of it. Let us proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said earlier, if this was translated correctly to me, that you did the forensic work, and you did not deal with the policies. Are you a forensic expert, sir?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: I'm an archeologist that specialised in forensic archaeology. So I am an expert not in all forensic matters, but I am an expert in forensic archaeology and to a certain extent in forensic anthropology. But when you ask am I a forensic expert in the broad sense, no. I don't know anything about DNA analysis. I don't know anything about finger-print analysis. But I do know how to excavate and apply it in the forensic scene.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do we agree that it is also not a part of your work to conduct autopsies and to establish the time and cause of death?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: It's certainly not -- it would not be counted as acceptable to me -- it would not be counted as acceptable in a court that I offered expert opinion on autopsies and time and cause of death. Yes, it's not part of my expertise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, in view of the time that I have, I'm just going to take one example, and this is your example of Glogova 1 from 2000. So where the description of the locality is, and this is the description of Glogova 1, that site, you stated that you noticed six areas where human remains were placed, as well as places where there were attempts of unauthorised re-digging in order to remove the bodies. Are you able to tell us anything else about these attempts? Were these just attempts or was this actually done?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: It was an attempt, but it wasn't a completed job. It was done, according to the aerial images, in October 1995. And a lot of bodies were taken away, judged by empty parts of graves we found. But also a lot of bodies were missed. So, yes, it was an attempt. Whether it was an attempt to remove all the bodies, I don't know, but they certainly didn't succeed in removing all the bodies. A lot were left. And a lot of body parts that had fallen off the bodies that were taken away were left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What I would like to know, however, is what would have happened with the conclusion regarding grave E had you dug deeper? Your first impression was that that grave was robbed and looted. It doesn't say looted, but it says that a number of the bodies were taken away. However, luckily, you said, "As we dug deeper, we concluded that that was not the case." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can we see the page? Doctor, if you found the page, let us know so that we can upload it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What is the page number, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, it's your report, and it's Exhibit P4009.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's page 6.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Page 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I think it's page 6, and the heading of that chapter is -- or section is "Description of Glogova 1 site."

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes. Now, in the case of -- I understand what you're talking about. In the case of grave E, that was not a grave --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Next page in English. Just a second. Grave E.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Grave E was a cave that -- a cave. Grave E was a grave that was not disturbed in October 1995. And the reason for saying that is both what we found in the excavations and also what the aerial images showed. The disturbance did not remove -- the disturbance did not touch grave E.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, you established that only after you dug deeper. Your first conclusion was that there was unauthorised digging and that the grave was robbed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Within the top parts of the grave we didn't find any bodies, but as we dug deeper we did find some bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did anything prevent you from digging deeper at all the other graves?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: No. My responsibility was, having starting the excavations at a grave, to ensure that every single body had been removed. To ensure that we did not leave any bodies behind, we always excavated below the graves until we got into natural soil. So even though, to go back to grave E, we didn't find any bodies in the top, we went down to the natural soil at the bottom of the grave, and that was when we found the bodies in grave E. But after we've finished emptying out a grave, we think it's the bottom, but we always remove soil to make sure that we are in the natural sail. And in my report on Glogova, I present as -- excuse me and minute, Mr. President. I present, on what is page 7 of the report, the natural soil that existed at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's go -- move two pages forward. Is this the page, Professor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, it is. And that is my reconstruction of what the soil was like before any graves were dug. And so we knew, therefore -- well, I say it's my reconstruction. We put in an excavation that was outside the area where the graves were to see what the natural soil was like. So in all those areas that are on my map of excavation of Glogova, we would have gone down to the natural soil to ensure that no bodies were left behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May I draw your attention to the next section where you talk about the digging and the robbing of the graves. This is the last-but-one paragraph where you state that you conclude that there is no reason for thinking that the bodies at Glogova 1 had been originally buried elsewhere, dug up, and then brought to Glogova. And you also then state: "On the contrary. The indications are that bodies were dug out of Glogova 1 and taken elsewhere." Were you able to establish that Glogova 1 was the actual site of execution?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: No. I didn't conclude that it was a place of execution, because unlike Kozluk, there were no shell cases lying around. There were some bullets with the bodies and I think possibly a shell case or two with the bodies, but they did not show -- there was not enough in the way of shell cases from rifles, pistols, to suggest that the bodies were executed at Glogova itself and then pushed into the grave. So I didn't think it was an execution site. On the other hand, there were no signs that the -- there were no signs, as there were at Cancari 12 and other sites, of soil -- of lumps of soil that were foreign to the area. What an archaeologist would look for, if you ask them, Are you sure these bodies were not buried in place A, dug up, and then taken to place B, such as Glogova? Then soil travels with the bodies. Soil is different from the local soil. We never saw that at Glogova, though we did see artefacts that were consistent with the -- anyway, bits of plaster and bits of the door frames, and so on, that were consistent with the bodies having been brought from somewhere else. And that somewhere else was, I concluded, the Kravica warehouse. But they had not been buried anywhere before. Mr. President, the transcript says that they had been buried anywhere before. I concluded it is that they had not been buried anywhere before, I said, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I kindly ask for your understanding. I'm just waiting for the Serbian translation to be completed before I put my next question to you. I would now like us to be more specific. How many primary gives did you find?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: In connection with those thought to be related to Srebrenica, I found -- or I worked at the Red Dam site, but that had been robbed. The only -- the next primary site was Kozluk, which we discovered because of the glass at Cancari 3. And the third primary burial site was Glogova. So in connection with these particular investigations there were three primary sites.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But only at one location, at Red Dam, you established that the primary gave was also the execution site; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: At the Red Dam there were enormous numbers of shell cases and bits of bone lying around on the surface of the -- of the area in which the grave was dug so that it appeared to me to be an execution site, and the bodies, I assumed, in the grave had come from that execution. But, of course, the bodies had been removed from the grave and only a few bones left. You ask -- yes, at the Red -- but it wasn't only one location that I established as a primary grave was also the execution site, because that is the core of my interpretation of Kozluk, that it was an execution site and a burial site. But Glogova was not an execution site. It was a place where people had been put as a first place of burial.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: They were killed somewhere else, thus; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: The people at Glogova were killed at -- not at the Glogova site, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How did you rule out that Glogova was a place of assanation [as interpreted]? How could you conclude -- how could you rule out the possibility that these were the bodies that were collected during the clearing of the terrain of soldiers who were killed in other places and that they were buried in that grave following the sanitation and hygiene measures?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't completely rule that out. My observations were that the -- not a single item of military clothing was found at Glogova. The bodies were buried in a -- a fresh condition and did not show signs of insect attack. Bodies that had been left out and then collected are normally attacked by blow flies, and the chitinous material of their bodies and wings survives well with the bodies. So these were not bodies that had been left out on a terrain, as it were, and then collected later. So I had no reason to suspect that there were -- there was a mixture of bodies that had come from various places.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, sorry to interrupt, but there's one transcript correction at -- on the previous page at line 16. The word "assignation," I believe, was meant to be the B/C/S "asanacija."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You're correct. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Professor, all I'm trying to do now is establish the following: Are you saying that all the corpses in Glogova 1 were of the same degree of decomposition? Or were there any differences in the stage of decomposition of the bodies?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Well, there were certainly differences in the stage of decomposition of the bodies, and that depended on where they -- where an individual lay in the mass of bodies. If you're buried in a mass grave on the very edge of the bodies, then you putrefy much faster and you're reduced to a skeletal stage much faster than the individuals in the middle of the mass of bodies. So they're not all in the same stage of decomposition, but the differences in the stages of decomposition are -- can be interpreted in terms of where the body lies in the body mass when excavated. The reason why I referred to the lack of any insect cases is because they are clues to -- if some bodies have insect cases and others don't, then that is a sign that these bodies have come from different places at different times. But we did not see anything like that. I saw nothing that required me to suppose that there had been several events behind these killings of the bodies at Glogova. I -- to my mind, they could be explained as from a single killing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's look at what you said in the chapter "Characteristics of the Graves and the Bodies." That is page 15 in my copy. And then you said: [As read] "The state of the preservation of the bodies varies from skeletonised to virtually fully fleshed. Figure 8. These differences in state of preservation are not to be taken as indicating different periods of burial." I don't know if in English it states "should not be or must not be taken." In Serbian what it says is "must not be." Are you able to tell us why these differences must or should not be taken to indicate that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes, I understand the difficulty of translation. What I mean there is that one shouldn't jump to the conclusion that these bodies were killed at different times, because we noted that these differences in state of preservation were due to the location of the bodies in relation to the main mass. I was not instructing people that they -- that this could not be the case, but that we didn't need to explain these differences in preservation other than in -- other than being due to location of the bodies within the mass graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: With your permission, I'm going to read that in English. I believe that it is translated correctly: [In English] "These differences it state of preservation are not to be taken as indicating different periods of burial."

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is that possibility ruled out, that they were brought in from different locations and at different times? And why would, in that case, such a possibility be excluded or ruled out?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: This is what I said earlier, that I agree that a second -- a different interpretation could be put on it but that it's not necessary to put that interpretation on the differential state of preservation. That's all I mean by that. In other words, I'm following a principle that you don't introduce new factors to explain what you're seeing unless you have to. In England we call -- in English we call it Occam's razor. But indeed I might -- for instance, if we found at the bottom of a grave skeletons and on the top of those complete bodies I would then say, I believe these bodies that had become skeletons were brought from somewhere else, it's a different event, because it is not possible, in terms of disintegration of bodies, for fresher bodies to be on top. But we didn't find anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, were you told where the grave was in which people who were killed in May of 1992 in Glogova were buried as a result of major fighting and apparently there were some unlawful executions? Were you told about this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: No, I was not told. I was not told to look for a grave that was believed to date from 1992, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you rule out the possibility that this grave that was formed in 1992, dead bodies were later buried in the process of sanitation and hygiene measures application?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Do you mean, Mr. Karadzic, that all the bodies were buried? Or that some bodies were buried later on top of other bodies?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, how many bodies did you find at Glogova 1?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Two hundred and -- no, 191 complete bodies and 249 body parts, in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, we do know that about 4 -- 64 people were killed in May in 1992. Did anyone draw your attention to that fact?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: No. I don't remember anyone telling me that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were also never told about the fact that there was fighting over those three and a half years, but also about the fighting in July. Those fightings took place in that area and lasted for about ten days. So that was an ongoing process.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Can I ask, do you mean July 1995 or 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: 1995, before and after the fall of Srebrenica. I'm talking about combat operations, not executions. So did you know that there was fighting in that period and that a large number of Muslim combatants used combat methods to achieve a breakthrough to Tuzla and that many of them were killed in the process?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of the history of those events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I note the time. It's time for a break. If you have more, then we'll take a break now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Certainly, Excellency. This is a very important witness. The Prosecution spent two hours examining him, and I hope I will be given at least six hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll have a break for an hour and resume at 1.35. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours, I'm not sure if you know, just to make clear: Unfortunately we do not have another witness for today, for the Court's information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And that's our understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. I just wanted to be clear. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 1.35. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.35 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Professor, you pointed out that in the case of Glogova 1 you found that quite a few people got killed by explosions or by explosive devices; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: I noticed two things at Glogova. And the answer is yes. But if I can just say, we noticed the -- why I said that, the bones were more broken than at other sites, and we also found explosive devices and bits of grenade and other metal embedded in some of the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I quite understand that you are reluctant to offer any forensic estimations as to the time and cause of death, but did you establish the age of the grave itself, i.e., the time when the grave was formed, as it were?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: I didn't establish it by my forensic investigations, but the aerial images show that the ground was not disturbed on the 5th of July, 1995, but that the ground had been disturbed by the 20th of July, 1995. So for those reasons I think that the age of the graves is established.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it possible to determine that at that same location no grave existed before and that new bodies were added which would lead you to believe that it was established in July? And I'm talking particularly about Glogova, for which we know for certain that there were killings in 1992 and 1993.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: There are two points I want to make in answering that question. Firstly, bits of the Kravica warehouse were mixed up with the bodies. There is no lower layer of bodies that doesn't have a mixture of bodies and bits of the warehouse. Furthermore, I'm familiar with graves, not at Glogova but elsewhere, where burials were made and then there was an interval of time and additional bodies were added. Now, the way we recognise that in the archaeological -- using archaeological methods is that if the grave is left open with the earlier bodies exposed, then there are insects that attack the bodies, and as I explained before, the chitinous material of insects is very durable and gives an indication that the bodies were exposed. Secondly, bodies that were left exposed get damaged very fast by the elements, the natural elements of climate. The bones begin to crack. On the surface, you get lines developing on the surface. Not breakage, but lines developing on the surface. At Glogova we never saw any sign of damage to an earlier layer of bodies. We never saw an earlier layer of bodies. Just to repeat, the bits of the warehouse were mixed up with these bodies. There was no earth, no soil, thrown over an earlier layer of bodies, and no sign of weathering or damage to the bone of any earlier bodies. I formed the conclusion, in the light of any other evidence, that we were looking at a singular incident of burial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Professor, you talked about the potential --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- the potential link between the Glogova site and the Kravica warehouse. Would you exclude the possibility of the -- bringing some part -- some bodies from the other -- other site, for example, so to speak, other killing site?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't exclude that, but what I would say, Mr. President, is they were included with the bodies from -- with the other bodies at the same time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said that -- if you allow me, I would introduce this new term that you mentioned, "robbed," such as the Red Dam, but can we call some other graves enriched? So did you find any graves that were enriched, so to speak, later on as opposed to those who you say were robbed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: No. I did not see any -- I understand the question and what you mean by "enriched." I did not see any graves which I interpreted as having been opened up for the purpose of depositing more bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But a while ago you said that you saw such graves where additional burials had been carried out. Was that only the Red Dam, or were any similar cases?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry, I didn't make myself plain. The graves that I saw were not to do with the case that we're talking about. None of the graves that I'm talking about fall into that category of graves to which bodies were added later. The graves in question, one of them is in the Ukraine and one was in the Prijedor area, which is not the subject of this -- of my testimony. I did not see any graves of this -- of the -- none of the graves that we're talking about now had bodies added to them, so far as my observations went.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Professor, it may have been the interpretation issue. Previously you said that you are familiar about graves, "not at Glogova but elsewhere, where burials were made and then there was an interval of time and additional bodies were added." But you don't see such examples in -- in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry, Mr. President, I didn't make myself plain. I didn't see it at Glogova. I didn't see it at any of the graves that are attributed to the Srebrenica event. But one of those graves that we're talking about I did see in Bosnia, but it was from the -- from 1992 killings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll get back to this. I remember you mentioning this in the context of the Red Dam. Now, let's finish with the issue of insects. Do you agree that on page 15 in the Serbian version you said that one should take into account the fact that the bodies were removed from the graves and that they were covered with mud which prevented one from seeing clearly all the characteristics of the bodies. Some of the entries in the body sheets were, therefore, provisional. In other words, the process of identification of dead bodies was finally completed in the morgue, because the final conclusions could only have come from the morgue. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We saw that it was mid May when we watched the video-clip. Can you tell us what was the temperature in those refrigerators?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: I don't know the temperature, but it would have been above the freezing point. And the ideal temperature would be about 5 degrees. But I don't know what temperature was actually achieved by the engineers. I should say 5 degrees Celsius.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And then you said earlier today that at times bodies were transported to the Visoko morgue. Can you tell us what were the intervals between those trips, when bodies were transferred?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: I should say an average time would be one week between the exhumation and their accumulation in the chiller van, and then they were taken down to Visoko and ... about a week, maybe less sometimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have any feedback information how long after the arrival the post-mortem was conducted?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: That I don't know, Mr. Karadzic. I went down to the morgue on a couple of occasions, but I didn't take part in their proceedings, and I don't know the interval between the arrival of the bodies and the carrying out of the post-mortem examination by the anthropologists and the pathologists. I can't comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it true that some of the graves, for example Cancari, were spotted in the images in 1995 and were only exhumed in 1998?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes. That -- that is the -- that is the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there a method of calculating the age of each particular grave or do we have to rely solely on the aerial images?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: To get any precision, yes, we have to rely on the aerial images. There are methods such as radiocarbon dating of the bodies would now, but not then, give us a rough idea of when the person died, but it would not have the precision of those aerial photographs. I perhaps should elaborate. The radiocarbon dating has been used for many years, but there's a particular form of radiocarbon dating that detects the radioactive carbon that was created by the hydrogen bombs that were let off in the early 1990s. And forensic scientists make use of the decline of this high level of radiocarbon to date bodies, and I've used this method myself in -- with the police in determining roughly when someone died and is found in the forest outside Sydney, and the radiocarbon labs were able to tell me it was between 1985 and 1992, but that's not very precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that there were intact bullets in pockets, but what I'm interested in is the Dutch newspaper that you mentioned. Was it possible to determine when those newspapers were dated? Or, actually, you said that there were pieces or strips of Dutch paper that were used to roll cigarettes. Was it possible for anyone to determine the date that those newspapers bore?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: I'm sure that would have been possible, but we -- I don't remember seeing a piece of that newspaper that actually carried the date of the newspaper, but presumably it would be possible, by reading the text, for somebody to determine when that newspaper was published, but I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have these artefacts been preserved?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: You would have to ask the investigators of the ICTY, because once I handed them over, I'm not responsible for them. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I ask my learned friend Mr. Mitchell, our -- since our printer is not working, I would appreciate if it would be possible to have the following documents printed: R108-63-9798, and this is at the same time my notification to the OTP that I'm going to use these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor, for your answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have a 65 ter number for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While this is being resolved, may I remind you of page 17 where you said that wounds were caused by shrapnel, by bullets, by hand grenades, and some other missile pieces. Also discovered were intact bullets in the pockets of those victims. Does this fact indicate that the person in question was actually a combatant?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Two things. Firstly, there was only one individual who had these rounds in his pocket, and that's illustrated on figure 17 of my report, and it was found with other personal possessions. But the fact that somebody has bullets in their pocket does not indicate to me that that person is necessarily a combatant, no. But I -- I can't -- I don't know anything about this person beyond that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, that's the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Is it to be given to the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two pages; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would appreciate if this be put on the ELMO, please. Oh, it seems that our printer is now working. It's been out of operation for about an hour. All right. Can this be put on ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I understand correctly, this is a letter of yours addressed to Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let us put that on the ELMO, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you recall this letter?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Can I, Mr. President, just read the letter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By all means, Professor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe we can put the other copy on ELMO for all the parties to see it. You can keep one hard copy for yourself, and let's put the other one on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't remember the details of the letter, but I acknowledge it is my letter, and I --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 3 there is mention of Article 90 of the Additional Protocols, and you said that had you been asked to apply that, you wouldn't have refused it.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: That's right. And I replied in that way earlier on to your questioning. But that's not because of my knowledge of Article 90. I don't -- I don't know what that Protocol says. I'm just saying there that had I been asked to allow an expert to the examination on mass graves, I would not have had any objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1974, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In relation to this paragraph that starts with the words "I agree that the exact number can only be determined by actual exhumations," would you agree that bearing into account -- bearing in mind four years of war and many people losing their lives, that that makes it even more complicated to estimate the number of cases that would involve deaths after the fall of Srebrenica? Maybe I made this way too complicated. There was a war going on and Srebrenica fell. Now, the question of making an estimate, hasn't it been made even more complicated? I mean, an estimate relating to the fall of Srebrenica. I mean, estimating the number of cases or the number of bodies, if you will.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: In dealing with the estimate of the number of bodies in the graves that were on those aerial images, I dealt with that in my answer to the prosecuting barrister. I said that I had checked later to find that those graves had been excavated and that my estimate of the number of bodies in the other graves was a bit of an underestimate. So that in dealing with the graves that were on the aerial images, I would stick by the method that I used in the report in 19 -- the report I made in 1999 on the 1998 season. Those estimates that are being criticised in this letter have since been shown to be reasonable estimates of the numbers of the bodies in the remaining secondary graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm not challenging that. This is what I'm interested in now: All of these bodies estimated to be in un-exhumed graves on the basis of average numbers, should they all be linked to the fall of Srebrenica, disregarding totally that there were four years of war before that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: I can only comment, Mr. Karadzic, on the graves that I personally excavated. What I was talking about in terms of the estimates are graves that I was not -- I did not excavate, and so I can't comment on the -- whether those graves bear on the question of Srebrenica other than by noting that they appear on the aerial imagery that was dating from July 1995. I -- I did not go back to Bosnia after the year 2000 when we finished at Glogova, and these other graves were excavated by other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, you do agree, don't you, that a far more accurate time of death can be established by way of a post-mortem rather than aerial images?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: I -- I doubt that, no. I think that even with people who have died in the last week there's considerable debate about the time at which they died. I think in this case if there are bodies and they're in graves and those graves are dated by the aerial images, as I understand what pathologists do, that would be a far better indication about the time of death of these people than anything that the pathologist could determine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But what shall we do with secondary graves? How do we establish when the people buried in secondary graves had died?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: We can only identify, as we did in many cases, the primary graves from which they came, such as Branjevo Farm, from the Red Dam, and the age of those graves is also known from aerial imagery. So the fact that they are in secondary graves does not mean that we can't date the primary graves from which they came. And I haven't made a detailed study of the aerial imagery at the time, but I've seen pictures of dated aerial images that are consistent with death in July of 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt again, Mr. President. Just, there was a suggestion a few minutes ago that the exhumations were somehow noncompliant with the Geneva Conventions. I'm just wondering if Mr. Karadzic could point to the exact provision that's being relied on there, because Article 90 has got nothing to do with the exhumation of mass graves. Article 120 of the third Geneva Convention does talk about the procedures to be followed after the death of POWs, but it doesn't mention anything about experts. So perhaps Dr. Karadzic would look into that and perhaps consider withdrawing that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Judge Lattanzi found Article 34, but I'm not sure whether it is the correct --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: And 90 also, 90 is fact finding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Rule 90 as well, Article 90.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Article 90, international fact finding commission --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are these the Additional Protocols? Are we talking about the Additional Protocols?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it Mr. Karadzic will come up with a more precise argument.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In principle, in the case of Markale and everything else, we asked for the Serb side to be present. However, we were always denied that. Perhaps this is a typographical error here in terms of how this article was copied. Can I just finish with Glogova now. You found -- you found 12 victims there with their hands tied, with ligatures on their hands; right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Somewhere else you found a few of those too. In Kozluk, somewhere like that; right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes, we did, and many in the secondary graves too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you were asked about what these were made of, you said cloth. Was it uniform or did it vary?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: No. I answered that I couldn't remember that, whether the cloth varied or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you certainly did not notice that this was a uniform matter, as it were.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Are we talking about Kozluk or about this grave at Glogova?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Professor, all the photographs we've seen that had to do with ligatures are different, and all of this seems to be makeshift. Whatever was at hand, they use it to tie these people's hands. It wasn't that some kind of uniform thing was manufactured for all cases.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: I didn't study the cloth, but I was told by one of the investigators who had studied the cloth that they - that's after the bodies had gone to the morgue - that there was -- there were many that were made of the same -- exactly the same cloth, but I can't speak to that point from my own personal examination of the cloth. I should also say that at grave L, at Glogova, which is the grave you're referring to where people had ligatures, that that was a polyethylene string and not cloth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You did deal with the number, didn't you? Not only establishing the exact number of bodies exhumed, but also you dealt with estimating the number of bodies in all the graves; right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes, I did give estimates of the number of bodies in all the graves in my reports, and also said that the final number would have to be determined at the morgue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you know that in different graves connections were being established on the basis of DNA?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes, I know that that was being done because I read about it, but none of that was started before I left Bosnia. It was all much more recent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not looking for any culprits here. I just want us to establish the following: If you agree that in Cancari 3 out of 138 bodies only 40 are connected with Kozluk, we cannot consider the rest to have been related to Kozluk; right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Well, you -- Mr. Karadzic, you're drawing on information there that I don't have, presumably from the DNA studies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. On the basis of DNA studies, the connections were being established between secondary graves, partial bodies, and so on. This connection was being established on the basis of DNA analysis. So, for example, in Cancari, 3 out of 138 bodies, only --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't you reserve that question for another witness. Dr. -- the professor said he's not aware of that analysis.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Professor, I am satisfied with your answer in terms of establishing the total number, but I'd still like to call up 65 ter 21024, a letter written by an investigator, Mr. Dusan Janc. 2009 or -- March 2009. There's also a Serbian translation here, but that's not it. Could I ask you to take a look at this text. Is it in line with what you said a moment ago, that this is no way to establish the number?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: I must have some time to read it, please. Yes, I've read it now. Could you ask me the question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this in line with what you said a moment ago, that these estimates cannot yield a number? The number has to come from the morgue -- rather, all the exhumations, and then ultimately the morgue.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes, I -- I think, though, that this correction by Mr. Janc relates to where the individuals in the graves came from rather than how the numbers are actually -- the numbers within the graves are actually calculated. It relates to origin of the bodies rather than the numbers of bodies that are in the graves. But perhaps I'm not understanding your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, in the penultimate paragraph it says: "Nevertheless, the exact number cannot be provided." Do you agree that if we're dealing with different locations, we cannot say that it's the same cause? Cause of death, I mean.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Certainly. If the DNA analysis has shown that most of the bodies in the Glogova mass graves came from the Kravica warehouse but some didn't, then I would expect them to maybe, maybe not, show different properties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This is going to be -- I understood to be tendered by the Prosecution. I would take it there's no position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. Janc is coming as a witness, so we could do it now or then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, why don't you reserve it when Mr. Janc is coming? I have no difficulty in reserving or admitting it as Defence exhibit, but this is --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, I'll tell you why. I offered part of Karavelic's statement here. The Prosecutor offered all of Karavelic's statement, thinking that they would call him as a witness. And I agreed to that because I thought that he would appear here. However, it was not fair, because they ultimately did not call him, so I will have to call him, and that is why I'm doing this now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I see no problem. We'll admit it. Exhibit D1975.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree, Professor, that the Serbs buried their own dead on their own territory through family arrangements, whereas victims from the other side were buried in mass graves, and the other way around? The Muslims buried their own victims with dignity, involving family arrangements, and they buried Serb soldiers in mass graves. Does this sound like a customary thing to you, and was that the way it was?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: I have no idea about the statement you're making to me, and I can neither agree or disagree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I were to tell you that part of Podrinje was under Muslim control for a while and about 50 mass Serb graves were found there and then when we liberated that area they were exhumed and these people were buried involving family arrangements, General Morillon attended some of these exhumations, does this piece of information shed more light on my previous question put to you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Could we have a date on this, just to put it into context?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was in 1993, the spring of 1993, when we liberated Serb areas that were held by the Muslims until then. This is a generally known thing, that there were about 50 mass graves, and that afterwards they had family funerals. And it was the other way around. Muslims buried Serb soldiers and Serb civilians in mass graves, and they buried their own by way of family arrangements. So it was the other way around as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karadzic, I never like to hear of atrocities that have been committed, but -- and I have no reasons to disbelieve what you're saying, but I must point out that I'm here as an expert witness about mass graves that I actually exhumed, and not to be an expert or give an opinion on historical events that I didn't investigate. I have investigated, under ICTY arrangements, the killing of Serb civilians in -- near Gospic, and that was a dreadful event, but I know about that, but I don't know anything about Eastern Bosnia, what was happening with mass graves there, other than those that I have been asked to investigate by ICTY.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. My intention is for us to have a look at this. You made a statement on the basis of 121 or 151, whatever, of the total number of bodies buried in mass graves in Podrinje, the Drina valley. Does all of this have to be linked to the fall of Srebrenica? How do we make a distinction in terms of those who have nothing to do with Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: I assume that by the Podrinje valley you mean Glogova, the site of Glogova. I'm not familiar with the geography in the geographical terms, but you do mean Glogova; yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Podrinje is the Drina River valley from Kozluk to Bratunac. The left bank of the Drina. All of that is the Podrinje. However, we call the area right by the Drina river "Podrinje." That is Kozluk as well, where you worked.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Well, I certainly made a statement that I found more than 121 or 151 bodies in the area that you're talking about. I found several hundred. How -- whether I can -- whether they relate to the fall of Srebrenica is, to my mind, fundamentally determined by the interpretation of the aerial images and, secondly, by the artefacts that we found within the grave. But they are, in my opinion, secondary to the aerial images which give dates for when those people were buried.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, Professor, but how can we know that the people who were killed in July 1995 were moved from a primary grave to a secondary grave? How do we know that they did not lose their lives before that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Because, as I said before, the primary graves themselves that we're concerned with are dated by aerial imagery, and so of course they lost their lives before they were put in the secondary graves, but I'm not aware of any primary graves that have yielded bodies in secondary graves and date from before 1995, before July 1995. I don't know of any.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not talking about the graves that you opened only. I'm talking about the method of providing this estimate. Do you allow for the possibility or do you rule out the possibility that in the secondary graves there were also bodies for which this was a primary grave?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: I interpreted the putting of bodies into the secondary graves as single events, and we saw no sign of executions around the secondary graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So this was not the execution site; right? However, do you rule out this possibility or do you allow for this possibility: that some bodies were added to certain graves? So for some bodies these are primary graves and for other bodies these are secondary graves.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: I don't think anything can be ruled out in these circumstances, but it would mean that we were very careless in our examination of the stratigraphy of the graves and the relationships between the bodies and differential decay and those other matters I mentioned before. The people -- members of my team are experienced in stratigraphic archaeology and in the effects on bodies of -- of damage to the bodies due to exposure and then other fresh bodies being added on top. So you asked me to rule out, but that is something which from the scientific point of view one is reluctant to say, but in fact I think it is beyond -- from my point of view, beyond a shadow of a doubt. I just do not believe that these were graves that -- that have been misinterpreted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Tell us this: You exhumed seven graves; right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: The seven secondary graves, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about the primary ones; nobody exhumed them, right? Your estimate, to how many graves did it actually pertain? You established certain things in relation to the bodies that you exhumed; however, you made estimates on the basis of this in relation to how many graves?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is starting to get a bit confused, I think. Are we talking about the estimate of 2.571 from the 21 probed graves? Is that the issue that we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't follow either.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, here it is. I think that the professor will know what I'm talking about. Some were exhumed, whereas for others estimates were made on the basis of the assumed average.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How many graves were left to have that done, that is to say, to have estimates made?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: I have explained before that I have checked -- well, can I go back to your original question, "What about the primary graves; nobody exhumed them; right?" The primary graves were exhumed. For instance, Branjevo Farm was exhumed in 1996, but not by my team. The primary graves to the south in the Nova Kasaba region were also exhumed in 1996, and I myself exhumed the major primary grave of Kozluk. So primary graves were examined -- exhumed. Now, as to the question of the estimates, I made an estimate in 1999 based on the 1998 work which you referred to. But as I have already told the Court, I have checked on the numbers of bodies that were in the graves that I didn't exhume, 21 secondary graves, and it turns out now in the light of actual exhumation of those secondary graves, those 21, that I slightly underestimated the number of bodies that might be in the graves that I didn't exhume.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, this is what I was counting on, these estimates. So the rest were exhumed by somebody else. Are you able to stand by the findings of these other experts who worked on the graves that you made assessments on but that you did not exhume yourself? Are you in a position or did you perhaps review their work and are you able to stand behind the results of their work?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Well, I certainly know the work of Jon Sterenberg. He worked for my team for four years and I've known him since, and he stayed on in Bosnia afterwards and worked for ICMP. I've always found him to be a person whose conclusions I could stand by. I don't know Mr. Dusan Janc, so I can't comment on his reliability. But I have no particular -- no reason to think that he's an unreliable observer, but then I don't know him, never met him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Fair enough, as they say. Is this a signal that it's time, that the time has run out? We still have a little time, doesn't we?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As long as you stick to relevant issues, I would allow you to continue as far as you can.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar or do you know what happened to the artefacts? What happened to the artefacts that you selected, as well as the artefacts in general that were exhumed during the exhumations?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: I didn't select any artefacts. There may be a bit of mistranslation. I found all the artefacts, and all -- I found the artefacts, and all of them are entered into the logs which were then given to ICTY, but the artefacts themselves were all sent down to the morgue, where, I understood, investigators carried out further analysis. As to what's happened to those artefacts, I have no idea in the sense of where they are now. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You found some ID documents, personal IDs, isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that it's a custom in our area that a prisoner of war or anybody who is captured would not be allowed to keep their documents, but they are forced to hand them over, otherwise they could escape?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: No, I have no idea about what the rules are in Republika Srpska. What they were, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And in your country is it possible for a prisoner to keep his passport?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, Mr. Karadzic, never having been arrested myself, I don't know whether I would be allowed to keep my passport or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It's my assumption that you're unable to answer the question that the person on whom personal ID is found would not have been previously arrested, but anyway, are you able to tell us whether Glogova 1 and 2 were mixed and whether the DNA that was found in those graves was also found in other graves? In six cases, for instance, it was proved that one body part was found there and another body part was found in a different location.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD WRIGHT
utterances.text: I don't know the facts of the particular case you're talking about, but it doesn't surprise me, given the way in which the bodies were handled, that a limb might fall off and be taken away in another truck which went to a different grave.
